title: Incident tool responses include Diagnoses without the diagnoses:read scope
description: A valid MCP Credential can be issued with incidents:read while omitting diagnoses:read. Both MCP scope layers deny that Credential's direct get_diagnosis call, yet list_incidents and get_incident return the complete stored incident object, including Diagnosis rootCause, evidence excerpts, confidence and references. The affected data belongs to the Credential's own Project; the crossed boundary is the delegated MCP capability for reading Diagnoses. The source trace retains Project isolation but contains no scope-aware removal of the embedded Diagnosis. The tool-layer boundary result was observed with dummy data inside the compliant container.

trace.description: An incidents:read Credential is admitted to get_incident while the distinct get_diagnosis mapping requires diagnoses:read.
The tool requests the complete incident view for the supplied identifier.
The backend requires Project context and parses the daemon response as RecordedHaunting, which allows a full embedded Diagnosis.
After daemon authentication and grant validation, the handler passes Project and id into the incident read.
The daemon reads the full durable Haunting through the private API using Project and id.
The correct composite Project/id query returns the recorded Haunting; it does not know the external MCP tool's scopes.
The mapper preserves the stored incident and its embedded Diagnosis while prepareRecordedHaunting redacts sensitive text.
The entire view is returned through deepRedact with no conditional removal of incident.diagnosis. listIncidents has the same projection at line 86.

evidence.description: The explicit primitive map separates incident-read tools from get_diagnosis and its diagnoses:read scope.
Issued Credentials store the requested narrow scope set. Verification returns record.scopes at line 122 rather than widening incidents:read to diagnoses:read.
incidents:read and diagnoses:read are separately issuable MCP scopes. Their shared canonical OAuth alias does not add the other MCP scope during Credential verification.
listIncidents returns sliced complete backend views; getIncident at line 94 returns one complete view. Neither receives scopes or removes Diagnosis fields.
IncidentSchema contains optional Diagnosis, whose schema at line 64 includes rootCause, evidence, confidence and createdAt.
RecordedHauntingSchema retains the full optional Diagnosis. prepareRecordedHaunting at line 100 preserves it while redacting rootCause and evidence text.
deepRedact recursively processes strings and keys, with no knowledge of the caller's capabilities and no Diagnosis-field removal.

root_cause: Authorization is applied to primitive names while the incident tools reuse the full RecordedHaunting response shape. That shape includes the very Diagnosis object protected by the separate get_diagnosis permission. Generic string redaction preserves the object and its nonsecret private content, so it does not enforce the missing capability at the response projection.
intended_behavior: A Credential holding incidents:read but not diagnoses:read must not receive Diagnosis content.

remediation.strategy: Project incident responses by the caller's MCP scopes, removing incident.diagnosis before deepRedact whenever diagnoses:read is absent; add a two-Credential regression test.

title: Concurrent Work attempts can reuse a stale Project PR-limit decision
description: An OAuth client holding tokens:manage and fix:trigger may start fixes for two distinct eligible Work items in its granted Project. With maxOpenPrsPerHour set to one and no recent publication, both attempts can read zero before either saves an intent. The source evaluates that counter before routing and patch preparation, then admits each publication using only its own Work/attempt/lease checks. The hypothesized result is two draft-publication admissions under the owner's one-per-hour policy. The two-admission result was observed with dummy Work items inside the compliant container. The actuator baseline reserves a durable single-use slot before execution; this fix path has no analogous Project-wide reservation.

trace.description: An authenticated management client with fix:trigger submits separate Fix now commands for two Work IDs; caller() supplies the principal's Project and actor. The same downstream policy path also handles automatic triage.
The daemon verifies the caller Project, checks replay and eligibility, claims the selected Work item and invokes runFix. Distinct Work items and command IDs do not share a Work fence.
Each live attempt resolves its own context before evaluating policy. No Project-wide publication slot is acquired at this point.
The daemon obtains shared policy facts from the API's Project-qualified internal context endpoint.
After the Project grant and Diagnosis checks, resolve requests publicationCount and returns it as counters.openPrsLastHour. This read does not reserve capacity for the attempt.
Only attempts in the Project with non-null publication and recent updatedAt count. Both claimed/running attempts can therefore observe the same zero while neither has reached beginPublication.
The daemon computes one open_pr policy decision from those facts and, after audit acknowledgment, continues on allow through routing and patch preparation without refreshing the PR counter.
The intended control denies an open_pr action when openPrsLastHour is at least maxOpenPrsPerHour. Two earlier zero snapshots both pass a configured maximum of one.
The acknowledged pre-effect audit is followed by runtime.beginPublication. Neither operation refreshes the earlier shared-cap decision.

The publication change runs in a serializable transaction after locking the Project/command pair. Different command IDs have different locks, and the transaction does not include the prior policy-counter read.

The durable boundary checks only this Work snapshot, active attempt, owning command, live lease and absence of prior publication; it then saves the publishing intent and audit. It never checks or reserves maxOpenPrsPerHour across other Work items.

Each admitted attempt reaches prepared.publish after its own saved intent. A bounded local fixture should stop at two mock draft-publisher invocations or two durable publication intents under the configured maximum of one.

evidence.description: Both fix triggers require policy allow before a draft pull request; this is an explicit owner policy boundary.
maxOpenPrsPerHour is a configured nonnegative integer limit.
The open_pr gate compares openPrsLastHour against that configured maximum.
The publication counter includes saved intents/known references but excludes attempts with null publication.
The source regression expects zero publications after claiming and one only after beginPublication; the test was read, not executed.
Policy is evaluated before routing and execute preparation; publication later uses that decision without another PR-count gate.
The strongest durable publication admission checks ownership, versions, live lease and saved intent, but not shared Project capacity.
Command locks include commandId and the serializable change transaction starts after the remote policy read; neither binds distinct Work publications to a cap reservation.
The production drain wrapper starts each command promise and tracks it in a pending set; it does not serialize commands. main wires this wrapper to createCommandHandler.
The actual publication sink runs after individual admission, with no additional Project PR-limit check on this path.

root_cause: The Project-wide policy count is read and evaluated outside the publication transaction. Claimed/running attempts do not consume publicationCount, and beginPublication neither rechecks the configured maximum nor atomically reserves a Project-wide slot. Serializable transactions, command-scoped advisory locks, the audit pre-effect acknowledgment and Work version/attempt/lease fences protect individual commands and Work records after the stale decision, so they do not bind publication to the shared limit that authorized it.
intended_behavior: The configured maxOpenPrsPerHour limit must bound Project-wide publication admissions.

title: Permanent Haunting-write failures retain expanding observation histories
description: A plugin Credential holder can send small valid detection Events with unique 180-character IDs. The public DTO and Event schema accept those IDs, but createObservations appends :detected:<rule> and sends that longer value to an internal DTO capped at 180 characters. Each write is therefore permanently refused after the accepted WatcherOutcome has entered the daemon's pending map. The consumer's five-delivery limit eventually stops retrying the broker record without notifying or evicting the cached outcome. With timestamps spaced by the watcher dedupe interval, later failed Events for the same bound service retain successive cloned histories containing one, two, three and more detections. This yields source-visible quadratic retained history across a linear number of small Events in the daemon shared by other granted Projects. No heap measurement, crash or service outage has been observed.

trace.description: A Credential holder can choose a nonempty 180-character low-entropy alphabetic ID. The small envelope fits the API size limit and can use its bound service.
Preparation and publication retain the caller's ID after Project/service authorization. An unassigned Event audit key with this ID still fits the core 200-character audit-key contract.
The watcher is mutated and its accepted outcomes are saved in pending before any durable Haunting write completes.
Each accepted detection extends signalIds and detections, then returns a structured clone of the entire cumulative group. Ten-minute-spaced caller timestamps permit successive accepted detections.
The daemon derives eventId by adding :detected: and the rule name to the already 180-character Event ID.
The internal record route rejects this derived value through MaxLength(180), which the global validation pipe reports as an unprocessable request.
Failed observation processing requests redelivery; the declared consumer caps deliveries at five but has no terminal-outcome callback to the observation cache.
The rejected reduction bypasses pending.delete at line 206. Cached cloned histories remain reachable for the lifetime of the observation runtime after broker retry exhaustion.

evidence.description: The pending Map has no declared size, expiry, cancellation or terminal-delivery eviction policy. Its only deletion is after successful processing.
The shared ID schema imposes only nonemptiness, so envelope preparation does not reject the public 180-character input.
Global DTO validation applies the internal maximum and uses HTTP 422 for validation failures.
The private API client throws for the 422 response, propagating failure out of observation processing before cleanup.
Five broker deliveries and bounded broker retention do not remove objects retained in the separate observation closure.
The default 65536-byte Event cap and 60-per-minute throttle bound individual input and arrival rate, but not lifetime cached outcomes. The proposed inputs are under one KiB each.
One observation runtime is passed to the shared granted-Project consumer, so retained state occupies the daemon used by other Projects.

root_cause: The in-memory pending outcome cache has success-only cleanup and no terminal-failure, size or expiry policy. Public Event-ID validation is incompatible with derived internal idempotency-key limits, supplying a deterministic permanent-error trigger. createGrouper returns a deep clone of each cumulative group, so each abandoned pending outcome retains its own history rather than only one bounded reference.
intended_behavior: A terminally refused observation must be evicted and must not retain growing cumulative histories.

title: A co-tenant Event can prevent release of another Project's closed Haunting group
description: When one daemon serves two granted Projects using the same service name, a Credential holder in Project B can submit a valid Event for that service (e.g. a warning 'http.request', a type unhandled by createRules, so no B detection is produced) while B has no active Haunting. The active lookup for B deletes the service-only byService cache entry belonging to Project A, but its attempted release is restricted to B and leaves A's watcher group intact. If A's durable Haunting is closed before its next eligible detection, that detection reuses the unreleased [A,service] group. The daemon loads A's closed record by ID, spreads prior.incident after change.incident so the closed state wins, and appends the new detection to that closed row rather than opening the fresh active Haunting expected by the existing single-Project close/reopen behavior (which the source test 'a persisted closed Haunting releases the old in-memory group for the next observation' exercises). The minimum claimed boundary result is a new Project A detection being recorded on a closed Haunting because of Project B's Event.

trace.description: A Project B Credential with events:publish may publish an Event whose body.projectId is B and whose body.service is a shared service name such as 'checkout' (project/service binding is checked at lines 31-35). A warning 'http.request' Event is schema-valid but unhandled by createRules, so it exercises the daemon active lookup without creating a B detection.

The daemon is booted with boot.projectIds (main.ts:71) and passes them as grantedProjectIds; processQueued admits any granted Project and serially invokes the single createObservations runtime registered at main.ts:115-155.

For B, the project-scoped active lookup (lines 79-83) returns null. old = byService.get('checkout') is A's incident ID; watcher.release(B,A-id) is called at line 93 and line 94 deletes byService['checkout'], losing A's cache ID while A's group survives.
release compares entry.projectId with the caller's projectId (B) at line 79, so it refuses to delete A's [A,'checkout'] group. A's stale group remains open while its cache entry is gone.

After A's durable Haunting is resolved, A's next eligible detection finds the still-open [A,'checkout'] group via the key at line 44, so add() at lines 64-75 does not call newId() and returns an 'updated' change carrying the old A incident ID and stale 'open' state.

The get-by-ID call at lines 107-111 uses A's projectId and the reused old ID, returning A's closed row. The spread at lines 123-131 places ...change.incident before ...(prior?.incident ?? {}), so the closed prior state overrides the stale 'open' state while the new detection and updatedAt are retained.

The authoritative row lookup is scoped by (projectId=A, id=old A id) at line 47; matching service/openedAt and monotonic updatedAt checks at lines 51-57 pass, so the tx.haunting.upsert at lines 61-66 writes the closed row's state back with the appended detection. No new active Haunting is created for A's detection.

evidence.description: byService is Map<string,string> keyed by service alone; its reads/writes/deletes at lines 50, 69 and 92-97 carry no Project component.
Open groups are keyed by JSON.stringify([detection.projectId,detection.service]), so the watcher and bridge cache disagree about identity.
active() at lines 98-105 filters state notIn ['resolved','dismissed'] at line 100 and scopes by projectId, so A's later null response is legitimate but the missing service cache ID prevents release.
mergeRecorded takes the next incident state (lines 69-76) and hauntingData writes incident.state directly to the row (line 48); there is no closed-to-new-detection lifecycle rejection.
The checks at lines 84-91 validate the returned active service, state and detection Project, but they do not scope byService itself, which remains service-only.
The single-Project test 'a persisted closed Haunting releases the old in-memory group for the next observation' confirms the intended close/reopen baseline that the cross-Project sequence breaks.

root_cause: createObservations stores active IDs in byService under service alone (lines 42, 50, 69, 92-97), whereas createGrouper stores open groups under [detection.projectId,detection.service] (pipeline.ts:44). Cache deletion, replacement and release therefore refer to different namespaces: B's null-active lookup deletes A's service-only cache ID while release(B,A-id) is refused by the grouper's Project equality check (pipeline.ts:79). Durable Project checks in HauntingRepo.upsert (haunting.repo.ts:28,47-57) protect row ownership and monotonic updates but do not repair the stale group, and haunting.mapper.mergeRecorded/hauntingData preserve the prior closed incident state on the appended detection.
intended_behavior: An Event from one Project must not corrupt another Project's Haunting lifecycle cache.

title: Collector evidence selection drops Project authorization
description: A caller holding an MCP Credential for one granted Project can select any service name for tail_logs and any daemon-allowlisted metric job. The API supplies the authenticated Project (the bearer guard enters it into McpProjectContext, and HttpMcpBackend.read includes it in the private daemon request) and the daemon checks grant membership, but the final collector reads no longer receive that Project: createReadHandler dispatches logs and metric without projectId, ReadRuntime declares logs(service,lines) and metric(promql) with no Project parameter, services(projectId) returns the entire global collector inventory with only an incident-state overlay, CollectorReads has no Project ownership contract, and the metric allowlist is derived from every configured job. In a deployment where one daemon observes evidence reserved for another Project or Organization, the source path would return that evidence using the daemon's Docker, Kubernetes or Prometheus authority. Redaction removes recognized sensitive strings but leaves ordinary private operational log text and numeric metrics visible. This requires a valid narrow-scope MCP Credential, a reachable real Project context, and a collector resource outside that Project's authorized scope; the cross-Project read was observed with a dummy sentinel inside the compliant container. The Event-driven diagnosis path reaches the same host-wide log reader: observations supplies an Event Project to its logs callback, but the production main callback accepts only (service, lines) and drops the Project before ReadRuntime.logs. Ordinary private log text can therefore enter the wrong Project's model context under the same ownership conditions, independently of an MCP HTTP context handoff. No provider request or persisted diagnosis was observed. Source review found no ownership predicate on any collector read path; the grant check, strict command schema, unique service match, namespace filter, exact PromQL allowlist and redaction constrain selection or content but do not bind the selected resource to the authenticated Project.

The daemon bearer, strict command schema and granted Project are checked; lines 89-93 then dispatch logs and metric without projectId.
The runtime finds the requested service in global collector inventory, requires one matching source and invokes tailLogs without an ownership query.
The Docker variant searches all API-visible containers only by serviceName; no Project value is available to filter the target.
The selected container id is safely URL-encoded and its logs are read using the daemon's configured Docker endpoint authority.
Returned log text is redacted and wrapped in untrusted_logs tags, then disclosed to the original MCP caller without checking the selected service's Project.

Collectors are bootstrapped with the first granted Project; lines 85-90 construct one shared read runtime from their sources and metric jobs, and lines 129-134 expose it to every granted Project.
The strongest Project gate is membership in options.projectIds. Lines 89-93 discard that Project for log and metric dispatch.
services(projectId) returns every inventory item and overlays only Project-specific incident state; logs selects global inventory and metric checks a global job-derived allowlist.
CollectorReads exposes inventory and log reads without any Project argument or ownership field.
Docker inventory includes all API-visible containers and log selection resolves only the service name.
Kubernetes filters a daemon-wide namespace list. Lines 171-185 enumerate those deployments and read a selected pod's logs without a requesting Project.
metricJobs contains all configured metric-target jobs, with no Project association.
The metric variant admits exact WATCHER_QUERIES for any configured job and invokes the shared metrics client. Exact query equality prevents arbitrary PromQL but does not provide tenant isolation.
The existing HTTP source test replaces MCP_BACKEND with a fake, so its success assertions do not establish the real bearer-to-backend Project-context handoff.
The adapter fixture substitutes McpProjectContext with a fixed Project, leaving production async-context propagation untested by that fixture.
The diagnosis path supplies service, 300 lines and the Event Project to its logs callback, then uses the returned logs in the Project-scoped diagnosis.
The production observation logs callback accepts only service and lines and calls the same Projectless ReadRuntime.logs method, dropping the Event Project.
Fetched logs become prepared diagnosis evidence; redaction and quotation validation do not add an ownership predicate.
The model adapter receives the prepared log context for the active diagnosis, establishing a source-visible alternate output path from the same wrongly scoped reader.

root_cause: ReadRuntime treats collector evidence as host-wide after checking only whether the caller's Project appears in the daemon grant. Its logs and metric methods have no projectId parameter, inventory is not filtered by Project, CollectorReads has no Project ownership contract, and the configured metric allowlist is global. The service uniqueness check and namespace/job allowlists constrain selection but do not bind the selected resource to the authenticated Project.
intended_behavior: Collector inventory, logs, and metrics must be authorized for the requesting Project.

title: Fix repository selection is not bound to the Work Project
description: A tenant able to publish evidence and initiate an eligible Fix in its own granted Project can name a service mapped by the instance policy to a repository outside that tenant's authority. contextClient checks the tenant's durable diagnosis and Deployment, but chooses the repository solely by service name. If the attacker registers a known commit from that repository as a Deployment in its own Project and the normal Fix policy allows the attempt, the daemon uses its operator GitHub App identity to fetch that repository for the attacker's Fix task. The affected resource is the other principal's repository/source context; the attacker need not possess a GitHub credential or membership in its owning Project. This candidate stops at the unauthorized repository-read/context-selection boundary and does not claim a verified patch, draft PR, merge or code execution. Independent source review of the same trace confirms: repository resolution uses only snapshot.item.service (fix-context.ts:42-46) while caller.projectId appears only in later durable reads/detections (lines 48, 64); RepoPolicy has no Project selector (types.ts:3-9; schema.ts:44-58); the final publication check repeats only service membership (open-pr.ts:36); and a caller-supplied Deployment SHA in its own Project (deploys.service.ts:30-56; DTO line 47 only checks 40-hex) supplies a syntactically valid commit point. Boot config is a single instance-wide PolicySchema with one github.repos mapping and one grant Project set (boot-config.ts:9-18; main.ts:94-99; internal-config.controller.ts:19-23); GitHub installation selection is keyed by repo string (auth.ts:95-97), not Project. The committed example config calibrates that this global service-to-repo mapping is the intended structural pattern, but that calibration is not grounds to dismiss the missing Project-to-repository authorization.

trace.description: With its own Deployment-write authority, the tenant registers a supplied 40-hex SHA in its own Project. The service checks Organization and Project access (lines 35-41), then appends the supplied SHA without repository ownership/provenance binding (lines 47-56). This is a required prerequisite, not a Deployment-authentication bypass.

The plugin producer supplies service, its own projectId and the registered Deployment. Scope, Project equality (line 31), optional Credential service equality (lines 33-35) and same-Project Deployment lookup (line 45) are enforced; the service is not resolved to a Project-owned repository.

The Event's diagnosed incident is saved in its Project (lines 181-189), converted to a Work item with that projectId (lines 191-199) and passed to onWork with that Project. A later eligible Fix remains a command on the attacker's own Work item.

The command checks the daemon Project grant (verify, lines 35-39), reads that Project's Work item (line 79), checks Fix eligibility (line 80) and claims an attempt (lines 81-84). The autoFix triage sibling reaches the same runFix path (lines 62-72).
The repository filter compares only repo.services with snapshot.item.service (lines 42-44). The unique match is selected (lines 45-46) before the subsequent caller-Project-bound context checks.

Strong diagnosis, service, confidence, category, detection-Project, signal and Deployment-SHA consistency checks bind the durable context (lines 55-72), but the returned repo is never checked against caller.projectId.
The open_pr decision and its audit must permit the attempt (lines 96-109). Its category/service/signal/counter gates (evaluation.ts:8-44) cannot supply the missing Project-to-repository grant.

After audit-scope, Deployment-SHA, base-audit (lines 80-105) and configured-verification checks (lines 108-110), the daemon passes input.context.repo, its GitHub client and the Project's Deployment SHA to prepareSource.
The claimed attempt resolves context with the authenticated caller and its Project-scoped Work snapshot (line 90).

Publication admission persists the chosen repo/branch/base under the caller's Project via beginPublication (lines 50-52) before invoking the prepared publication (line 55); it does not add a repository ownership check.
The last repository allowlist gate checks incident.service against repo.services and the patch path rules, with no Project selector.

client.getCommitTree(repo.repo, baseSha), followed by tree/blob reads (lines 191, 204), uses the instance GitHub identity without caller Project information. This is the minimum resource-authority boundary requiring validation.

evidence.description: One daemon grant supplies a Project set (line 21) alongside a single instance policy and Agent list (lines 22-23), rather than a policy/repository mapping for each Project.
Repository entries contain repo, services, base branch and patch constraints (lines 45-57), but no Project owner/grant. Rule matching (lines 10-26) also lacks a Project selector.
Repository selection is the unique service-name match; caller.projectId is used only in later durable API reads (line 48) and detection checks (line 64).
Deployment creation requires the tenant's legitimate org:ci or project:write authority (line 64). The candidate does not assume another Project's Deployment can be borrowed.

title: Publication recovery can accept a same-parent head with unverified content
description: A repository actor able to rewrite a generated bot branch can replace its head with a different tree whose sole parent is the admitted Deployment SHA. If the draft is still open and the attempt needs reconciliation, recovery checks the current PR head against the current ref and original parent, then records that draft as the completed Fix. It never compares the remote tree to the verified patch. The branch name includes verified hashes, but a writer can retain that name while changing its content. The affected boundary is Graveshift's verification/result authority: the claimed effect is acceptance of an unverified draft head, not GitHub write privilege gain for a writer, automatic merge, or release execution. Branch permissions and a bounded acceptance result remain unvalidated.

trace.description: An authenticated replay of an uncertain publication parses the persisted intent containing repo, branch and baseSha, with no expected result tree or head. The lower-trust input is the current remote branch/PR state a repository writer can have replaced.
Recovery forwards only the recorded repository, mutable branch name and base SHA to the GitHub client and checks the returned repository/branch.
The client requires a unique open draft with the exact head ref in the same repository, preventing fork/ref confusion but not modification of the named branch.

It reads the remote commit's SHA and parents plus the current ref. The schema omits tree identity; acceptance requires only matching current head/ref and one parent equal to the recorded base. A different tree with that parent satisfies these checks.
The returned head reference is recorded under the original attempt and base. API recordPublication checks intent repository/branch/base and known-reference equality, not the verified tree.

The Work attempt is finished as completed with ok:true and the recovered head, without rerunning source verification. The minimal result to validate is recording a harmless substituted tree as the verified Fix.

evidence.description: planPublication validates the local receipt but returns only repository, deterministic branch and original base SHA.
Snapshot and patch hashes influence the branch name; they are not independently recovered from remote content.
The durable PublicationIntent schema has no expected head, expected tree or verified content digest.
The strongest remote check verifies PR head/ref consistency and a single parent equal to baseSha, with no content-identity comparison.
The normal publication path also returns a recovered existing draft immediately, without creating the verified content again or checking its remote tree.
The durable consumer checks repository/branch/base equality and fences state, but accepts the first recovered head because the intent has no expected content identity.
Source tests exercise wrong base, merge/root commits, moved refs and mismatched heads; no same-parent/different-tree binding is represented. These tests were not executed.

root_cause: The immutable object identity is lost when planPublication reduces the receipt to repo/branch/baseSha and PublicationIntent persists only those fields. getExistingDraft binds the current head/ref to the base parent but does not bind its tree or head digest to the original verified result. Both existing-draft reuse and uncertain-effect reconciliation trust this weaker identity.
intended_behavior: Draft recovery must verify the same immutable content identity that was originally verified.

title: macOS verifier cleanup targets one process group instead of all descendants
description: When a configured verification command executes repository-controlled code on macOS, that code can attempt to start a detached child in another process group. The source sandbox permits child creation, but the supervisor kills only the original command group. A descendant retaining inherited stdout can keep the close event and verification promise pending beyond the deadline; one using ignored stdio can instead remain alive after a successful return and during parent workspace inspection. This crosses the untrusted-check lifetime boundary into shared daemon work/process resources. The candidate is limited to retained work and potential concurrent writers; no host-file disclosure, actual service exhaustion or sandbox credential escape has been demonstrated.

trace.description: A policy-accepted patch or repository file is executed by an operator-configured verification command. This condition requires a command that actually executes repository-controlled code; Git diff-only checks do not provide it.
The platform chooses sandbox-exec with macProfile. The policy permits process-fork and same-sandbox child operations, without Linux's PID namespace.
The trusted supervisor starts a detached command group with piped stdout. Repository-controlled code can attempt to create another detached group and retain the pipe or ignore stdio.
Cleanup and the timeout signal only -child.pid. They do not enumerate or own the detached descendant group, and the timer does not independently reject the promise.
Completion waits for close, which can remain pending while a separate descendant holds stdout. Conversely, ignored-stdio descendants need not prevent close and are not proven dead before returning.

While the verification promise remains pending, the attempt scope can continue its lease heartbeat; its finally block has not run. A closed-stdio survivor instead overlaps verifyPatch's post-command workspace inspection.

The daemon retains and drains pending Work promises, so a verification operation that outlives its deadline can also retain graceful drain. The minimal bounded observation is one dummy descendant or operation surviving a short deadline, not a stress test.

evidence.description: The sole termination target is the original negative child PID/process group.
The timer sets timedOut and calls stop but does not reject or resolve a still-open child result independently.
Only close resolves a running command; waiting on inherited stdout is therefore outside the timer's direct control.
The macOS policy permits process-fork. Unlike the Linux branch's --unshare-all path, it does not create a process namespace or bind all descendants to a supervisor-owned lifetime.

An existing source test intentionally spawns a detached child group from a sandboxed process and explicitly signals that group itself. It does not test supervisor cleanup after the parent exits or times out; the test was not run.
Host-side assertWorkspace follows a returned command, and finally removes the root at line 229 without a proof that every descendant has exited.
The HTTP handler bounds waiting with within(result), but the underlying command promise remains owned by drainCommands; this does not supply descendant cleanup.

root_cause: sandbox.execute treats process.kill(-child.pid) as complete teardown and resolves only from child.close. The macOS sandbox profile allows fork and same-sandbox child groups but supplies no descendant supervisor or process namespace. Changing session/group therefore falls outside the only kill target, while neither the timer nor verification independently terminates the pending operation or proves all writers are gone.
intended_behavior: Every verification descendant must be terminated before workspace inspection and cleanup.

title: Password changes leave other pre-change Account bearers usable
description: A holder of a copied, still-valid Account bearer can continue using it after the legitimate Account holder changes the password, for the remainder of the one-hour token lifetime. For the bootstrap Account, a bearer issued while mustChangePassword is true also becomes owner-capable when somebody else completes the password change. The source has no session-specific state that distinguishes the current caller's bearer from another holder's bearer. The stale-token acceptance was observed with two dummy sessions inside the compliant container; it requires prior possession of a valid token and stops at authority within that Account's own Organization.

trace.description: An Account login before the password change issues the bearer later held by the attacker. The attacker must already possess this valid token.
The bearer contains Account sub/email and a 3600-second expiry, with no session identifier or password-version binding.
The legitimate holder uses a separate session to change the Account password; the service verifies the current password before writing the new hash.
Only passwordHash and mustChangePassword are updated. No bearer-revocation state is changed.

The old bearer still passes signature/audience verification before expiry. The stored Account exists, and its current mustChangePassword false value removes the first-login restriction for all such bearers.
The stale bearer supplies the same Account id, whose existing owner Membership and same-Organization Project satisfy the otherwise correct authorization checks.
A holder of the pre-change token can create a new Project-bound OAuth client under the Account's Organization without knowing the new password.

evidence.description: Account token issuance binds only sub/email, static issuer/audience/key and one-hour expiration.
Changing the password correctly requires the current password, but the successful path does not revoke or rotate pre-existing bearer state.
The password write changes only passwordHash and mustChangePassword.
The strongest current-state controls reload Account and Memberships; they do not compare token issue time/version with the password change. The first-login gate uses the Account's current boolean.
Account has no session version, password-change time or revocation relation that the guard could consult.
The existing test expects a pre-change token to work after the root password change. This was read as source, not executed, and does not cover invalidating a separately held token.

Clearing mustChangePassword therefore affects every unexpired token for that Account, including separately held first-login tokens. Preserving the current password-changing session may be intentional, but this representation cannot invalidate other sessions separately.

title: Kiro shell hook guard guesses the event shape and fails open outside a finite command denylist
description: The tracked `block-dangerous-shell` hook runs `node scripts/kiro/guard-shell.mjs` on every shell tool call. The script does not bind to any in-repo Kiro event schema: it reads stdin, heuristically JSON-parses it, probes eight guessed field locations for a command, and on a read error, an unrecognized shape, or an empty string returns '' and exits 0, which the repository's own documentation says allows the tool. The sibling `secret-scan-on-save` hook repeats the shape-guessing pattern and also fails open, reading an arbitrary path from event JSON. The only statements of Kiro's exit-code contract and hook principal are repository-authored; no vendor schema, payload fixture, or runtime source is present, so exploitability depends on facts outside the repository.

title: Docker restart selection can cross Compose project boundaries
description: When a Blessing is intended to restart one Project's worker service, a caller holding that fresh signed request can potentially cause the actuator's Docker identity to restart unrelated worker containers in other Compose projects on the same daemon. The writer selects all running containers with the service label and invokes restart for every returned ID. The request can remain exactly as approved and correctly signed; the unresolved issue is which resources that service name resolves to. This requires an enabled act-mode configuration, shared-daemon co-tenancy, per-project approval intent and a proxy that exposes both projects. The checked-in configuration is propose, and the in-repo platform-to-actuator producer is deferred. The wrong-target restart fan-out was observed with a recording backend inside the compliant container; deployed exposure remains owner/conditional.

Admission checks the approval identity, action/incident binding, time, policy and action count for the signed service name.
The explicit target allowlist compares ctx.service to rule service strings and cannot distinguish different Compose projects with the same service name.
A successful unique token/action claim commits before execution. This correctly prevents replay of the request but does not narrow its resolved container membership.
The backend receives only action.service; no Project or Compose-project identity is supplied.
The Docker list filter contains only com.docker.compose.service=<service>. The returned set is not checked against another ownership predicate.
The actuator sends POST /containers/<Id>/restart for every returned ID under the host proxy's Docker authority, potentially including the unrelated project's same-named service.

The signature covers the entire accepted action, approval and context, which prevents tampering but cannot bind a resource scope absent from that object.
The sole lookup predicate is the Compose service label; lines 38-46 restart every returned container.
The production launcher instantiates this backend from DOCKER_PROXY_URL without an additional Project or Compose-project binding.

The maintained actuator proxy mounts the host Docker socket and enables container access, POST and restarts. No project-specific filtering is expressed here; effective image and deployment behavior remain unverified.
The committed default mode is propose, so activation of the runtime sink requires an owner-reviewed act-mode configuration.

title: Runtime admission substitutes zero for authoritative policy usage
description: In a supported act-mode configuration, a submitter holding a still-valid signed Blessing issued before usage limits were reached can potentially execute a restart after recorded diagnosis-loop or Project daily-spend limits require denial. Runtime admission supplies zero for those quantities instead of obtaining current recorded usage, while the canonical policy gate applies both limits to runtime actions. Correct HMAC, an allowed human approver, target allowlisting, safe scale bounds and the local runtime action count remain required. The affected boundary is the admission owner's current policy decision under the actuator's Docker or Kubernetes authority. The shared helper is used by both the active local SQLite path and the optional API claim path. The denial bypass and stub backend invocation were observed inside the compliant container.

Strict parsing and HMAC verification authenticate the action, approval and available context. The signed context has no authoritative usage counters.
The active store obtains its clock and per-service action count and calls admissionDecision. It has no dependency that reads recorded diagnosis-loop or daily-spend usage.
The helper passes zero diagnosisLoops and zero llmSpentTodayUsd into the canonical policy engine, irrespective of the real recorded state.
This gate denies runtime actions when either actual usage quantity reaches its configured limit, but the substituted zeros pass positive limits when the other checks pass.
A require_approval decision from the incomplete facts becomes no denial reason, allowing the valid human approval to satisfy admission.
The token/action claim is committed under the incomplete policy decision and reported as claimed.
The late check covers approval eligibility and breaker state only; it does not fetch usage or restore the omitted policy gate inputs before run is invoked.

For a valid Docker restart action, the privileged backend sends the container restart request even though a policy decision with the recorded usage would require denial. This final result remains to be demonstrated with a recording stub.

Diagnosis-loop and daily-spend limits are unconditional gate terms after the runtime-versus-PR rate-count choice. They therefore apply to runtime actions.
The strict signed context permits only category, signals and confidence, so even an honest request producer cannot provide these omitted facts through the current wire contract.
The production local admission path obtains only the per-service runtime action count before invoking the shared runtime decision.

The optional API claim path calls the same runtimeDecision helper after counting action claims; it does not resolve Project/incident policy usage either. This is a source-visible sibling variant of the same root cause.
The authoritative context path reads recorded usage for the granted Project, service and incident and includes it in SharedPolicyContext instead of assuming zero.
Recorded usage derives daily Project model spend and per-incident diagnosis-call counts. Parsing rejects unknown or invalid costs, establishing that unavailable usage must not silently become zero.
The post-claim eligibility recheck covers breaker and approval checks only, so there is no later authoritative-usage check that prevents the proposed effect.

title: A permanently rejected workload name can block the shared Collector queue
description: An enabled Kubernetes Collector watches multiple configured namespaces through one ordered queue. A less-trusted workload owner who can choose a legal name containing a dummy model-key-shaped substring, such as demo-sk-aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa, can produce a Warning Event that maps to an observation whose service fails privacy validation. The queue retries that deterministic failure forever, blocking later observations from other watched workloads. The Docker variant uses a producer-controlled com.docker.compose.service label containing a dummy email such as ops@example.invalid. The affected resource is the Collector's observation lane; no process crash or suppression beyond that Collector is claimed. Each variant requires delegated workload metadata authority and normally functioning Collector publication; the head-of-line result was observed with two dummy records inside the compliant container.

The helper passes Context.service into prepareEnvelope, preserving the workload-derived selector as routing metadata.
The model-key detector matches the dummy sk- substring and rejects the non-UUID service with EnvelopeError on every attempt.
The same permanent validation exception is caught and retried with capped backoff until the queue is externally stopped.
The worker never reaches acknowledge, pending.shift or notification for the poison head, so later unrelated workload records cannot publish through this Collector.

Service and fingerprint are privacy-checked routing metadata rather than redacted payload fields.
A full queue aborts the push watch, but finally waits on queue.drain; this cannot bypass a permanently failing head or reconnect to healthy later records.

The Docker variant trusts the com.docker.compose.service attribute for service and constructs its envelope inside the same retrying delivery callback at lines 99-110. An email-shaped label deterministically fails the separate email metadata detector.

title: Allowed telemetry strings may cause superlinear synchronous redaction before truncation
description: A producer holding a service-bound plugin Credential can submit a valid Sentry event with a long alphabetic event.type below the one-MiB envelope limit. The mapper redacts that entire string before truncating its normalized type to 128 characters, and its payload projection can omit the original top-level type. The shared email detector has an unanchored greedy local-part expression that can repeatedly scan suffixes of a non-matching token. This creates a source-grounded candidate from one Project's telemetry capability to CPU work on the shared API process; the final Event can be small enough for the broker cap. Plugin payload and identity processing reach the same detector under the smaller plugin request cap. No timing, service interruption, or cross-Project delay was demonstrated, and no severity is assigned.

The route accepts a raw envelope up to one MiB; it does not impose a separate maximum on the JSON event.type string.
The parser checks whole-envelope and event-item byte caps and parses an event JSON object without a per-field string-length bound.
The accepted event object is passed to mapSentryEvent before final envelope validation or broker publication.
The raw exception type or event.type is passed to redact in full at line 25; the 128-character slice occurs afterward at line 28. A long top-level event.type is not copied into the mapped payload.
The synchronous detector loop calls String.replace for the email expression on the API request's execution path; the maximum of four passes does not limit the work of one match attempt.

The unanchored [A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+ local part followed by a required @ can rescan successive suffixes of a long non-matching alphabetic token. Engine behavior and meaningful shared CPU delay require bounded validation.

The email pattern is /[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}/g, with no preceding token boundary or explicit local-part length bound.
redact invokes detector passes synchronously and has no cancellation, worker isolation, or elapsed-work budget.
The Sentry raw-body limit is one MiB; this is an effective input-byte control but permits a long single type token.
The parser independently enforces the default whole-envelope and event-item byte limits before event mapping; the candidate must remain within both.
Both ingestion controllers use the configured client throttler. A meaningful proof must use a single admitted request, rather than rely on bypassing or exceeding the rate limit.
Plugin events have a 65,536-byte default and 102,400-byte configuration ceiling; the adjacent throttler defaults to 60 requests per 60,000 ms.
The plugin sibling reaches redact through recursive payload cleaning; privacy.ts also applies the same detector set to metadata using hasSensitiveText.
The declared 128-KiB stream message limit is downstream of the Sentry type redaction and can still admit the mapper's small final representation.
The API bootstrap starts one Nest application listener. The reviewed redaction path executes in that application, without a source-visible per-Project worker boundary.

Sentry eventType invokes it before the only type-length truncation. The strongest visible controls are the one-MiB Sentry raw/parser caps, the plugin default 65,536-byte and maximum 102,400-byte cap, client request throttling, four redaction passes, and a downstream 128-KiB stream message limit. They bound request count, total bytes, passes, or final publication size, but do not establish linear regex work or preempt a synchronous call. Whether the supported Bun engine optimizes this pattern enough to prevent meaningful shared impact is unresolved.

title: Caller timestamps can grow temporal watcher arrays without a bound
description: A plugin Credential holder can submit unique small warning log.line or runtime.restart Events for its bound service while keeping observedAt at one valid timestamp. Each unique Event passes the replay set, and every saved timestamp remains inside inWindow because the comparison uses that same caller timestamp. The error/restart array is then filtered and copied on every input without saturation at the detection threshold. The downstream ten-minute dedupe prevents repeated emitted detections but runs after this work and does not cap sample retention. Source therefore gives linear retained samples and quadratic cumulative array work for a linear number of accepted Events, even when arrival rate respects the API throttle. The shared serial consumer makes this a possible cost imposed on other Projects; no measured delay or availability failure is claimed.

The shared daemon forwards each newly identified warning Event to watcher.ingest with the producer timestamp unchanged.

Distinct IDs bypass replay suppression. The bounded observed Set does not limit per-service arrays, and at is parsed directly from observedAt.
All prior samples equal to at satisfy time > at-windowMs and time <= at, regardless of elapsed wall time. Every input scans the full retained array.
The filtered array is copied and appended with no count limit. runtime.restart repeats the same pattern at line 94, retaining growing arrays in the shared watcher's per-service state.

Body and rate limits exist. They do not impose a lifetime sample quota or require producer timestamps to track the arrival clock.
The one consumer awaits each Project's processing serially, making per-Event growing array work part of shared observation dispatch.
prepareEnvelope validates format and redacts content but preserves the caller-supplied observedAt unchanged; no server time is substituted, so the timestamp driving inWindow is producer-controlled.
